newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich sees Dole tax cut in balanced budget plan.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich sees Dole tax cut in balanced budget plan.

text.p: Republican leaders in Congress have agreed to make Bob Dole's $548 billion tax-cut proposal part of a revived plan to balance the federal budget by 2002, House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich said on Monday.

Promising no significant changes in Social Security and Medicare, the Georgia Republican said the plan could impose a freeze on most other government programmes, including defence, while keeping overall spending growth at 2 percent a year.

"The only way the tax cuts move is in a bill that has a balanced budget, exactly as we did in December of '95. In December of '95, we passed a balanced budget with tax cuts, and sent it to Bill Clinton, who vetoed it," he said.

Gingrich told a news conference the plan to twin tax cuts and a balanced budget had won the agreement of Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich and Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici.
"If Bob Dole is elected and we're in charge in 1997 there will be one bill. That bill will have six years of spending, six years of tax cuts and it will be balanced in 2002," he said.

"It was 3,000 pages in 1995. It will probably be between three and four thousand pages this time. And you will get one vote one time, so if you want the tax cuts you have to vote for the balanced budget. If you want the balanced budget, you have to vote for the tax cuts."

The Republican balanced-budget plan last December led to a bitter standoff between President Bill Clinton and leaders of Congress and brought two partial federal government shutdowns, for which Republican leaders suffered most of the blame.

Dole's new tax-cut proposal, aimed primarily at families, stirred worries about ballooning federal deficits of the kind wrought in the mid-1980s by Republican President Ronald Reagan's tax cuts. But Gingrich said economic growth would be enough to compensate for Dole's tax cuts while bringing the budget into balance.

"You increase government 2 percent a year. That allows you to increase Medicare and Social Security without any significant change and it allows you to pay interest on the debt," he said. "You then take everything else including defence and you have what we call a flexible freeze at about $1 trillion this year. And at the end of six years you've got about $1 trillion."
Democrats argue that the Republican plan depends on promises of economic growth that are unlikely to be met.
